770: Difficulty identifying or naming what you are feeling
772: “Have I been reacting emotionally differently from usual?”
773: “Do I feel more… or less than is normal for me?”
776: Some people say “I’m fine”, but the body shows the opposite. The body often expresses what we have not yet been able to put into words. You may notice:
777: Constant tiredness or a feeling of “drained energy”
778: Difficulty sleeping or sleep that does not restore you
779: Frequent headaches or a feeling of pressure
783: Tightness in the chest or shortness of breath
784: Physical agitation (restlessness) or, on the contrary, slowing down
785: “Has my body been giving signs that I have been ignoring?”
786: “Do I feel physically different from my normal?”
787: How I think and organise information
789: Distress also affects the way we think and interpret the world. You may notice:
792: Racing thoughts or a feeling of a “full mind”
794: A tendency towards negative or catastrophic scenarios
796: Intense self-criticism or a negative inner dialogue
797: A feeling of confusion or lack of mental clarity
798: “Do I find it hard to stop thinking?”
799: “Have my thoughts been more critical or negative?”
800: What I do or stop doing
802: Changes in behaviour are often among the most visible signs. Some people switch off and avoid, others speed up and do not stop. You may notice:
803: Isolation or withdrawal from colleagues and relationships
804: Less involvement in tasks or loss of motivation
806: More mistakes or difficulty maintaining performance
807: More impulsive reactions or more conflicts
808: Working too much to avoid stopping (hyperfunctioning)
809: Doing less of the activities that used to bring pleasure
811: “Am I avoiding things that I used to do easily?”
812: “Am I doing too much… or too little?”
815: Distress is also reflected in how we connect with people. You may notice:
816: Less patience or more irritation with colleagues
818: A feeling of being misunderstood or distant
820: A greater need for validation or reassurance
821: More frequent or more intense conflicts
823: “Am I more distant… or more reactive with others?”
827: More than isolated signs, what matters most is to observe:
831: ImpactIs it interfering with how you function?
832: This way of looking is not meant to alarm or to pathologise normal reactions to stress, but to raise awareness and allow a more timely and appropriate response.
833: The sooner a person recognises that something is not right, the greater their ability to mobilise resources and look after themselves effectively.
835: A · When to ask for support
836: Asking for support is a form of self-care and not a sign of weakness.
837: Although it is natural to go through periods of greater stress, it is important to recognise when the distress becomes persistent, more intense or starts to interfere with how you function.
838: Areas in which signs can appear
844: It may be important to seek support when you recognise several signs in these areas.
846: An important sign: persistence and impact
847: More than a single sign, it is important to observe:
848: 1whether these changes persist over several weeks;
849: 2whether they are getting more intense;
850: 3and whether they are starting to interfere with your functioning, wellbeing or relationships.
851: Seeking help in good time can reduce the impact of distress and make it easier to return to greater balance and wellbeing.
852: If you recognise several of these signs
853: It may be an indication that you need additional support, whether from people you trust or from professionals.

868: What helps me keep my balance
869: Before turning to immediate strategies to cope with stress or anxiety, it is important to have a consistent regulation foundation in place. Looking after this foundation does not remove difficulties, but it helps you deal with them more effectively. 0 of 4 seen

874: Managing demands and limits
876: Emotional balance starts in the body. Deficits in rest, food or hydration have a direct impact on how you think, feel and react.
877: Sleep: keeping a regular, restorative sleep pattern is essential for emotional and cognitive regulation.
878: Food and hydration: eating a balanced diet and staying well hydrated contribute to steady energy and less reactivity.
